Chapter 25

The booking page

Service, person, day, time, details — in one page that survives a refresh and works without JavaScript.

By the end of this chapter

The public flow, with state in the URL and the details form hidden until it is relevant.

Five decisions, one page, no wizard. Each step appears as the one before it is answered, and the whole thing is one scroll on a phone.

The URL is the state

Every choice before the time itself lives in the query string: ?service=cut-and-finish&with=<staff id>&day=2026-10-20. None of it is $state. Each value is derived from page.url, and each is checked on the way in — with must be somebody who offers the service, day must be a real calendar day that is not in the past (parseIsoDate, from the time layer, returns null for anything else) — so a stale or hand-edited link falls back to "anyone" and "today" instead of asking the server for something it will never offer. Even the visible week is derived: weeks are counted in sevens from today, so the strip always contains the chosen day.

Putting the choices in the URL buys three things for free: a refresh does not lose the customer's place, the salon can link straight to ?service=cut-and-finish from Instagram, and a customer can send a friend the exact day they are looking at. It buys a fourth that matters more than all three: every choice is now a plain link, so the page works before its JavaScript arrives, and without it at all.

Every link on the page comes from here. resolve() takes a route ID with a query string attached, so [slug] is still filled in and type-checked, and URLSearchParams does the encoding. The if (!params.slug) guard has a story of its own in the comment above the function in the real file: during a navigation away, the outgoing page renders once more with the incoming route's props, and resolve() throws on a missing parameter.

Two SvelteKit 3 changes sit behind these lines, and the comments in the file explain both. page.url is a ReadonlyURL — its searchParams has no set, and assigning to pathname throws — which retires the old habit of copying the URL, poking the query string and handing the copy to goto; building the link from the choices with resolve() is the replacement. And the data-sveltekit-reset="false" you will see on the day strip below is the link form of the one reset option that replaced SvelteKit 2's noScroll and keepFocus pair, because wanting one without the other was almost always a mistake.

A day is a link

The strip draws links and owns no state: the page passes the days to show, the one that is chosen, and hrefFor, a function that turns a day into a link with everything else in the URL kept. Its type is (day: IsoDate) => ResolvedPathname | undefined, and ResolvedPathname is what resolve() returns, so only a link built by resolve() fits — and the svelte/no-navigation-without-resolve lint rule can see that inside the component.

With JavaScript, SvelteKit turns a click into a client-side navigation, and the two attributes on the strip shape it. data-sveltekit-reset="false" keeps the scroll position and the focused link, because throwing a keyboard user back to the top of the page for every day they look at would be cruel, and the link they pressed is still there afterwards. data-sveltekit-replacestate replaces the history entry instead of adding one, so Back leaves the time picker rather than replaying every day that was looked at. Without JavaScript both are ignored, the link is a page load, and the server renders that day's times.

Why links, and not buttons with role="radio"

The strip used to be a row of <button role="radio"> inside a role="radiogroup", with a comment claiming the role "gives arrow-key navigation for free". It does not. ARIA roles describe behaviour; they do not add it. A screen reader announced "radio button, 1 of 7", the user pressed the arrow keys as a radio group invites, and nothing happened, while every day was its own Tab stop. The buttons also did nothing at all without JavaScript, inside a form this course calls progressive. A list of links needs no keyboard code because it uses the keyboard behaviour links already have, aria-current marks the chosen one, and the chosen day is styled from [aria-current='true'] itself, so what is seen and what is announced cannot drift apart.

Revealing the form at the right moment

A form asking for a name and email while the customer is still deciding which Tuesday is noise. Worse on a phone, where it pushes the actual choice off the screen. So the details stay out of sight until a time is chosen, and animate in when one is, which also tells the customer something happened without a message saying so. Between the heading and the button sit a one-line summary of the chosen time, the error alert from the end of this chapter, and the four fields: name, email, phone and a note.

The section is always rendered, and the CSS rule decides whether it shows. :has() asks the browser whether any time in the grid is checked; the radios are rendered by SlotGrid, another component, hence the :global(...) inside it. The selected that the summary reads is chapter 23's derived value: the chosen slot, if it is still one of the times on screen.

Why CSS, and not {#if}

This section used to sit inside {#if selectedStart !== null}, where selectedStart came from the form field's value. With JavaScript, fine. Without it, that value is whatever the server rendered — nothing — and it never changes, so the name, the email and the Book button were never in the page at all, and a checkpoint in this course that told you to book with JavaScript disabled could not be passed. Whether a radio is checked is something the browser knows by itself, script or no script, so the rule that reveals the form now asks the browser. A browser without :has() shows the details all the time: a worse layout, and the same working form.

Not asking questions with one answer

If only one person offers the service, there is no question to ask, so we do not ask it. This is the kind of thing that separates software that feels considered from software that feels like a form.

When there is a question, it is an "Anyone" link followed by one link per person who offers this service, each the same page with ?with= changed, built the same way as the day strip's and for the same reasons: it works without JavaScript, survives a refresh, and is a Tab stop that Enter follows. offeredBy is a $derived in the script — the team filtered to the people who offer this service — rather than a .filter() written into the {#each}, so the markup says what it lists and the script says how.

Two clocks, honestly labelled

Times render in the visitor's zone, because that is the clock they will be looking at when they need to leave the house. The studio's time is shown only when the two zones actually differ and a slot has been chosen — saying "that is 14:00 at the studio" to somebody standing in the studio's own city is noise, and saying it before they have picked anything is noise with no referent.

The server does not know the visitor's zone on the first render, so it uses the studio's and the browser corrects it after hydration. Do not "fix" that by hiding times until hydration: a page whose content appears a beat late is worse than one that adjusts, and it is empty to a search engine.

When the answer is no

Most refusals are the schema's — a missing name, an email that is not one — and they arrive on the fields themselves. The handler's own refusals are about the chosen time: it was taken, it fell inside the notice period, it is past the booking horizon, the person no longer does it. REFUSED_TIME is the set of those BookingError codes, and each goes on the form with invalid(issue.slot(…)), attached to the slot field. Only a studio or service that has vanished is a failure screen, because nothing on the form can fix that.

The page shows that sentence beside the grid, where the remedy is, once the refused time has left the screen — which it does by itself: the live grid drops a taken slot within moments, and one that has slid inside the notice period at the next minute's tick, and the selection derived from it goes too. Without JavaScript the page that comes back is rendered without it. Choose another time and the alert gives way; the details below were never cleared, so the name and email are still there.

The same rule as chapter 21

This handler used to call error(409, …) for a lost race, which sent the submission to +error.svelte: a failure screen whose only button is "Back to the start", and a customer typing their name and email in again to try a different time. That is precisely the mistake chapter 21 corrects on the sign-in form — a refusal the person can put right on the same form belongs on the form — made a second time, on the page where it costs a booking.

A lost race is rarer than it sounds, because availability is a live query: a time somebody else takes disappears from the grid, usually before the customer reaches the button. When one does reach the server, the loser is normally turned away by the re-check at the top of createBooking, because the write queue lets the winner commit first, and the sentence is "That time is no longer available." Only two server processes racing each other get as far as the claim table, where the loser hears "Sorry — that time was booked moments ago." Either way it is the same answer on the same form.

The race is made deterministic by running the loser with JavaScript off. That browser picks a time and fills in its details; a second, ordinary browser books the same time with the same stylist; then the first presses Book. With no script there is no live grid to drop the time first, so the submission really does reach the server and lose — and the page that comes back is the booking form, with the sentence, without the lost time, and with the name still filled in.

Checkpoint

Choosing a service, a person or a day updates the URL; refreshing keeps all three; the details form appears only after a time is picked; and with JavaScript disabled the whole flow still works, from the service list to the confirmation page.
